title: Do It Again: Replication
objective: After this level you can explain why one study is rarely enough and what happened when scientists tried to repeat published results.
summary: Luck can pass a 5% test, so one study is a clue, not proof. When 100 psychology studies were repeated in 2015, 36% of repeats were significant against 97% of originals.

cards.headline: Scientists redid 100 published studies. Most weren't significant again.
cards.body: It happened in 2015, and every one of the originals had been published in a psychology journal. So why would a repeat fail? The answer starts with what a single significant result can and can't tell you.

cards.headline: Luck passes the test sometimes
cards.body: Level 67's 5% line has a built-in catch. If nothing at all is going on, a test will still come out significant about 5 times in 100 by chance alone. Fisher saw it coming in 1935: no single experiment, however significant, can prove a natural phenomenon. What counts is knowing how to run an experiment that will rarely fail to give a significant result.

cards.headline: The big repeat
cards.body: In 2015, a large team called the Open Science Collaboration put published findings to that test. They repeated 100 experimental and correlational studies from three psychology journals. Of the originals, 97% had statistically significant results. Of the repeats, 36% did. And on average, the repeat effects were half the size of the original ones.

cards.fact: One study is a clue. A repeat is how you check it.
cards.context: Replication is how science sorts sturdy results from lucky ones. In the 2015 project, whether a result came back was better predicted by how strong the original evidence was than by who ran the original or repeat studies. Strong evidence tended to hold up; weak evidence tended to fade.

cards.headline: Replication
learned: Luck passes a 5% test about 5 times in 100
One study is a clue, not proof

questions.prompt: When the Open Science Collaboration repeated 100 psychology studies in 2015, what share of the repeats came out significant?

options.rationale: Far from all: most repeats weren't significant.
97% is the share of the original studies that were significant.
Half is the size of the repeat effects compared with the originals, not the share.

questions.explanation: 97% of the originals were significant, but only 36% of the repeats.

questions.prompt: Why can't a single significant study settle a question?

options.label: Journals only print one study per topic
options.rationale: Journals print many studies; the issue is chance.

options.label: With no real effect, about 5 tests in 100 still come out significant
Significance wears off as a study gets older
options.rationale: Results don't decay; lucky ones just fail to repeat.

options.label: A single study can't include a control group
options.rationale: Single studies can have control groups; chance is the problem.

questions.explanation: At a 5% line, luck alone makes about 5 in 100 tests significant when nothing is going on. A repeat shows whether a result was one of them.

questions.prompt: In Level 9, a 1992 team measured body temperature again and got 98.2°F, not the famous 98.6°F. What were they doing?

options.label: Checking an old result by repeating the measurement
Running the first-ever body temperature study
options.rationale: Wunderlich's study came over a century earlier; they were re-checking it.

options.label: Converting Celsius to Fahrenheit more carefully
options.rationale: They took new readings, 700 of them, rather than redoing the arithmetic.

options.label: Testing a new fever medicine against a placebo
options.rationale: No treatment was tested; they re-measured healthy adults.

questions.explanation: Taking fresh measurements to see if an old result holds up is replication: one study is a clue, a repeat checks it.
